topics.title: 12.1.1 Distinguishing Replicated Decisions from Broadcast Messages
topics.summary: Broadcasting a message to several machines does not establish that they agree on one committed order. Recipients can miss different messages, restart at different times, and disagree about which sender was authoritative. Consensus addresses agreement under a defined failure model, with safety and progress conditions that depend on the protocol’s assumptions.

topics.title: 12.1.2 Separating Safety from the Conditions for Progress
topics.summary: Safety asks whether conflicting committed decisions can occur. Progress asks whether an operation eventually completes when the required conditions hold. A protocol can preserve safety by declining to proceed when it cannot obtain sufficient authority. That behavior may be operationally inconvenient but is different from returning an unsafe success.

topics.title: 12.2.1 Treating Lease Expiration as an Authority Event
topics.summary: A lease grants authority for a bounded interval under the coordinator’s rules. Its expiration can let another participant obtain authority. It does not forcibly stop the previous holder’s CPU, revoke every buffered I/O operation, or erase a delayed request already in the network.

Neither setting substitutes for a resource-side authority check.

topics.title: 12.2.2 Understanding Why a Distributed Mutex Is Not a Process Stop
topics.summary: A mutex in one address space controls participating threads that obey its protocol. A distributed lock similarly controls participants only through its defined interfaces. It cannot prevent an old process from writing directly to an unrelated storage API that ignores the lock.

cards.question: Explain Understanding Why a Distributed Mutex Is Not a Process Stop in your own words.
cards.answer: A mutex in one address space controls participating threads that obey its protocol. A distributed lock similarly controls participants only through its defined interfaces. It cannot prevent an old process from writing directly to an unrelated storage API that ignores the lock.

blocks.text: Not every external service supports fencing. An email provider or physical device may expose an API without a generation check. In that case, the architecture needs a different authority boundary, an idempotency facility, a serializing adapter, or a carefully stated limitation. Renaming an advisory lock “exclusive” does not create enforcement.

topics.title: 12.3.1 Designing Monotonic Fencing Checks
topics.summary: The local model keeps the highest accepted token. A write with a smaller token is rejected. A write with an equal token is allowed because the current holder can perform multiple operations; a larger token advances the accepted generation. The comparison and state update belong in one atomic resource operation in a real implementation.

topics.title: Failure clinic — Check-then-write leaves a race
topics.summary: A client asks the coordinator whether it still holds the lease, receives yes, and then pauses. The lease expires before the client writes.
